what_it_does: Doing math inside the memory chip itself — rather than shipping data to a separate processor — is an attractive way to break the bottleneck between memory and computation. But these in-memory processors (one name for them is PIM — Processing In Memory) each only see their own small slice of data; if a workload needs all processors to share partial results (for example, summing up contributions from every memory bank, called 'all-reduce'), the data must travel through the host CPU, which becomes a chokepoint and defeats much of the speed advantage. PIMnet is a dedicated communication network wired directly between in-memory processors, letting them send data to each other without routing through the CPU at all. The network mirrors the physical layout of the memory chips: there is a fast lane between banks on the same chip, and a separate lane between chips. Critically, the in-memory processors themselves manage this network rather than the host, so the extra hardware cost is kept small while collective communication patterns (summing, broadcasting, scattering) become much faster and more scalable.
